passage: With a tight food budget and one gas ring in the shared flat, Harsha, who had just started cooking for her flatmates, could not afford a ruined big batch of dal. So she filled four small pots with a cup of dal each and changed one thing in each: an extra pinch of turmeric, a little more cumin, lemon at the end, a tempering of garlic. Ankita, a flatmate, tasted each from a steel spoon and said, 'Number three.' Harsha wrote on the back of an envelope: cumin plus garlic. Pots one and four went into lunch boxes so nothing was wasted. Next day Harsha made a full pot with that mix and it tasted right.

qa.q: How many small pots did Harsha fill?
What was Harsha afraid of when choosing small pots?
qa.a: Harsha was afraid of ruining a big batch on a tight budget, so she wanted cheap trials that could be undone.

qa.q: What other approach could Harsha use to remember the recipe?
qa.a: Harsha could measure the spices in spoonfuls and write the amounts down, since a written recipe makes the good pot easy to repeat.

qa.q: How might Ankita have seen the tasting?
qa.a: Ankita probably enjoyed being part of it, and gave a clear choice by saying 'Number three.'

grounding: Shows a new cook trying spice changes in several small pots of dal instead of one big batch, so mistakes are cheap and reversible.

passage:
Kalyani had cooked exactly three meals in her life before moving to Bengaluru for her first job. On Sunday she wanted to learn dal the way her grandmother made it.
Instead of one big pot, she cooked a cup of toor dal and split it into four small steel bowls.
"Why four?" asked Manoj, her flatmate's brother, visiting for the weekend.
"Because if I ruin one bowl, I've wasted a spoon of dal, not a whole pot," she said. She added a pinch of hing to one, more jeera to another, a dry red chilli to the third, and extra turmeric to the fourth, then tasted each with a clean spoon.
"Chilli one's closest," she said, writing it on the fridge list. "Next Sunday, chilli plus hing."

qa.q: How many small bowls did Kalyani split the dal into?
qa.a: She split it into four small steel bowls.

qa.q: Why did Kalyani choose four small bowls instead of one pot?
qa.a: She felt safe experimenting that way, reasoning that ruining one bowl wastes only a spoon of dal, not a whole pot.

qa.q: What else could Kalyani do to make her next trial even more useful?
qa.a: She could note the exact pinch or spoon she used in the winning bowl, so she can repeat it and build on it next Sunday.

qa.q: How might Manoj see Kalyani's four bowls?
qa.a: Manoj is curious and perhaps amused at first, then may see it as a clever way for a new cook to learn fast without much waste.

grounding: It shows a new cook testing spices in several small bowls of dal, since cheap and reversible trials let her explore without much waste.

"Four tiny pans? Ayesha, you'll wash dishes all night," Vikas said, leaning on the kitchen counter.
"Better than ruining dal for twelve people." Ayesha stirred the first pan. "Khala is coming on Friday. If I make one big pot and get the tadka wrong, that's it. This way I try four versions with a cup of dal."
"And then?"
"Then I taste and pick." She added garlic to one pan, curry leaves and mustard seeds to another, ghee-fried onion to the third, nothing extra to the fourth.
Vikas tasted. "Curry leaves one."
"Hmm. Garlic one is better." She laughed. "Fine, we try garlic plus curry leaves tomorrow. Still only a cup."
"You'll be a chef by Friday."
"No. I'll just know what not to do."

qa.q: What was Ayesha worried about if she made one big pot?
qa.a: She was worried about getting the tadka wrong and ruining dal for twelve people.

qa.q: What else could Ayesha do after finding her favourite version?
qa.a: She could cook the final recipe once at full size before Friday, to check that it tastes the same in a big pot.

qa.q: How does Vikas see Ayesha's four pans?
qa.a: Vikas teases her about the dishes but joins in tasting, and ends up impressed, joking she will be a chef by Friday.

grounding: It shows a new cook trying several small pans of dal with different tadkas, since cheap reversible trials let her explore quickly without waste.
